title: Blackstone Says India Is Nearing a Tipping Point for Foreign Capital
excerpt: Jon Gray told Bloomberg Television that India now generates Blackstone's best private-equity returns in the world — a reversal from the years it "did basically nothing" there.
body:
• Blackstone president Jon Gray told Bloomberg Television's Wall Street Week that India is "getting closer and closer to that tipping point" for foreign capital inflows.
  • India is now Blackstone's highest-returning private-equity market in the world, after the firm pivoted to majority-control stakes in IT services, commercial real estate and domestic manufacturing.
  • The investment case rests on scale: GDP of $3.69 trillion — up nearly fivefold since 2005 — 7.6% growth in fiscal 2026, 1.47 billion people, and 11 million college graduates a year.
  • Gray credited improving infrastructure, legal systems and capital markets — and praised the Modi administration's economic stewardship — as the drivers pulling global capital toward India.

The interview

Blackstone sees India approaching an economic tipping point for foreign capital, according to the world's largest alternative asset manager's second-in-command. In an interview with Bloomberg Television's Wall Street Week that aired this weekend, Blackstone president Jon Gray said two decades of investing in the country had turned it into the firm's strongest private-equity market by returns — a remarkable reversal from the years the firm, in his words, "did basically nothing" in India.

"It takes time to get to a stage where you can really begin to expand your growth rate," Gray said. "And I do feel like India is getting closer and closer to that tipping point."

A reversal two decades in the making

Gray was candid about the false start. "We had sort of a skeleton crew. We didn't really have a great defined strategy," he said. "We couldn't make the numbers work. So we did basically nothing." The global financial crisis then slowed plans further. The turning point came when Blackstone changed its approach: "We said, 'You know what? We just need a better approach.'"

"We had sort of a skeleton crew. We didn't really have a great defined strategy. We couldn't make the numbers work. So we did basically nothing."

— Jon Gray, president, Blackstone, on the firm's early years in India

The firm stopped relying on minority positions and shifted to majority or equal-control stakes, concentrating on information-technology services, commercial real estate and domestic manufacturing. That pivot converted India from an afterthought into Blackstone's top private-equity market globally by investment returns. Gray noted the firm has been a control-oriented investor in India for years — a weighting he has previously called one of Blackstone's best decisions in Asia.

What "tipping point" means concretely

Gray's tipping point is not a prediction that foreign money floods in tomorrow. It is the claim that the preconditions for compounding foreign investment are nearly all in place: physical infrastructure, functioning legal and capital markets, and a deep talent pool. Ranked 14th in the world in a 2005 World Bank report, India's gross domestic product has grown almost fivefold to $3.69 trillion, climbing to fourth place — above Germany, the United Kingdom and France. Growth accelerated to 7.6% in fiscal 2026, the World Bank reported, keeping India the world's fastest-growing major economy.

The demographic case is the one investors keep coming back to. India is home to 1.47 billion people and surpassed China as the world's most-populous country in 2023. Mohandas Pai, the former Infosys CFO, noted that 11 million people graduate from college in India every year. A separate write-up of the interview by Business Today reported Gray praised the Modi administration, saying it had "done a phenomenal job" on the economy. The Economic Times summed up the turnaround with its own headline: Blackstone once came close to giving up on India; now it calls the country its best bet.

What investors should watch

A tipping point is only useful if capital actually crosses it. Inbound foreign direct investment into India has been uneven in recent years, and portfolio flows remain sensitive to global rates and the rupee. Gray's framing suggests Blackstone expects the consistency of returns — not a single blockbuster year — to do the recruiting: once global allocators see India's risk-adjusted returns holding up across cycles, the allocation models adjust themselves.

For NRI and India-focused investors, the signal is practical rather than patriotic. Gray's argument is that India is shifting from a "promise" trade — buy the demographic story and wait — to a "compounding" trade, where control investors can deploy at scale across sectors. India also ranked first for business climate among 41 markets in the Global Business Climate Survey 2026, with 61% of surveyed firms planning to raise investment within 12 months. Watch the next quarterly FDI data, state-level industrial policy (states are competing aggressively on regulatory easing), and whether the capital-markets deepening that underpins Gray's case survives the next global risk-off episode.
image_caption: A Blackstone sign stands outside one of the firm's offices. Blackstone executives say India is nearing a tipping point for foreign capital inflows.
nri_angle: For NRI investors weighing India allocations, Blackstone's verdict reframes the trade: the world's largest alternative asset manager says India has moved from a long-dated demographic promise to its best-performing private-equity market on actual returns.
author: Diaspora Desk
